text.p: Cambodia's beleaguered co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Sunday accused his coalition government rival Hun Sen of trying to destabilise his royalist FUNCINPEC party and stage a "real coup d'etat."

Co-Premier Hun Sen of the Cambodian People's Party (CPP) fuelled tension between the partners in the ailing coalition by pledging full backing and assistance for FUNCINPEC dissidents challenging Ranariddh's leadership of the royalists.

He claimed on Saturday that 12 FUNCINPEC MPs had split with Ranariddh and would give the CPP and two smaller allies a majority in parliament for the first time, enabling them to pass legislation in the 120-member house.
The CPP would need a two-thirds majority to change the constitution, dismiss senior government officials and lift the immunity of MPs.
"The matter is very, very serious it is a real coup d'etat, not only the constitutional coup d'etat, but staging the real coup d'etat," Ranariddh told reporters at a World Cup soccer match.

"I will go further later on, be patient. We will have enough evidence and I will ask (FUNCINPEC's armed forces deputy chief of staff) General Nhiek Bun Chhay along with me to tell you exactly what was planned," the prince said without elaborating.
He said Hun Sen was trying to destabilise the country through the destruction of FUNCINPEC.

FUNCINPEC is going through its most serious rift since opposition leader Sam Rainsy was expelled from the party and parliament in 1995 for criticising the coalition government of FUNCINPEC and the CPP.
Sam Rainsy, ironically, formed an alliance earlier this year with Ranariddh, while Hun Sen has become the prince's bitter foe after more than a year of feuding.

One FUNCINPEC official claimed that eight of 11 MPs named in a statement released at Hun Sen's press conference on Saturday had returned to the Ranariddh camp. FUNCINPEC on Friday expelled five of the dissidents, including leaders Ung Phan and Toan Chhay.
Ranariddh and his supporters have accused Hun Sen of engineering the rift.

Serei Kosal, special advisor to Ranariddh, later told a press conference that "a number of FUNCINPEC MPs have been threatened by armed people at their houses, a number of FUNCINPEC MPs have been forced by Hun Sen to sign the statement.

"We think this is a flagrant act against human rights," he said, adding that they had complained to the local representative office of U.N. Commission on Human Rights and the head of the parliamentary commission on human rights, Kem Sokha.
FUNCINPEC officials claimed between 40 and 50 MPs were sleeping at the party headquarters because they were worried about harrassment from the CPP.

Ties between the two premiers, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-organised elections in 1993, have lurched from crisis to crisis since a March 30 grenade attack killed up to 19 people at a rally led by Sam Rainsy, who has blamed Hun Sen.

Tension has also been heightened by the unsuccessful attempt by former FUNCINPEC secretary general Prince Norodom Sirivudh to return home from exile to fight his 1996 conviction on charges linked to an alleged plot to kill Hun Sen.
